subject: medicine
title: Cardiomyopathies and myocarditis

steps.tx: Dilated cardiomyopathy presents with breathlessness, ankle swelling and a third heart sound from systolic failure, and echocardiography shows a dilated cavity with **low ejection fraction**. Ischaemic disease, sustained alcohol intake, peripartum timing and persistent tachycardia are reversible triggers to identify, while **cardiac resynchronisation** helps selected patients with wide left bundle branch block. Screen first degree relatives with echocardiography, consider genetic testing for lamin disease, track symptoms with natriuretic peptides, and refer advanced cases for transplantation or durable support.
steps.say: Echocardiography confirms a dilated thin walled cavity that contracts poorly, so ejection fraction falls while breathlessness and ankle swelling develop. Doctors search for coronary disease and ask about alcohol intake, while recent delivery and persistent fast rhythm point toward reversible triggers. Relatives need screening echocardiograms because familial variants pass through families and early detection changes management. Selected patients with broad conduction delay improve after resynchronisation pacing, and advanced failure moves toward transplantation assessment when medicines no longer control daily symptoms.

vis.alt: Dilated cardiomyopathy is a big thin-walled cavity with low ejection fraction; hypertrophic is asymmetric septal thickening of 15 millimetres or more with a murmur louder on Valsalva; restrictive is a stiff normal-thickness ventricle with biatrial enlargement from amyloid, iron or sarcoid.
vis.caption: Dilate, thicken, stiffen: cavity, wall and filling tell the three apart.

steps.tx: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes asymmetric septal thickening with systolic anterior motion, and the murmur grows louder with Valsalva strain while easing when the patient squats. Exertional **syncope and family history** of sudden death mark high risk disease, and **atrial fibrillation** needs anticoagulation because stroke risk stays high. Risk scores guide defibrillator implantation for prevention of sudden death, while septal myectomy resects muscle and alcohol ablation infarcts the septum when gradients cause symptoms. Screen young athletes carefully since collapse on the field can be the first warning.
steps.say: The septum thickens asymmetrically and obstructs outflow, so the murmur strengthens during Valsalva strain and softens when squatting increases preload. Fainting during exertion alarms doctors, especially when relatives suffered sudden death at a young age. Atrial fibrillation demands anticoagulation because clots form readily in the enlarged atrium. Formal risk scoring decides who receives a defibrillator, while surgeons resect muscle and cardiologists ablate the septum when gradients produce limiting symptoms. Athletic screening matters because collapse during sport sometimes announces the disease.

steps.tx: This systolic parasternal image shows a markedly thickened **interventricular septum** measuring about 15 mm, with labels marking the aorta, left atrium, mitral valve and left ventricle. The arrow toward the outflow tract reminds examiners that obstruction here produces the **dynamic murmur** which changes with posture and strain. Correlate the picture with bedside findings during Valsalva and squatting, then confirm gradients with Doppler echocardiography and arrange family screening. Recognising this pattern helps candidates link anatomy, murmur behaviour and sudden death prevention in one view.
steps.say: The scan displays the long axis of the heart during systole with the thickened septum clearly measured on screen. Labels identify the aorta and the left atrium, while the mitral valve sits beside the narrowed outflow path. Obstruction at this point explains why the murmur shifts with Valsalva strain and squatting. Examiners expect candidates to connect the picture with bedside signs and Doppler gradients. Family screening follows diagnosis because relatives may carry the same inherited thickening.

vis.caption: Parasternal long-axis echocardiogram in systole showing thickened interventricular septum. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Restrictive cardiomyopathy produces a stiff ventricle of normal wall thickness with enlarged atria, and **cardiac amyloid** enters the differential when carpal tunnel syndrome or tongue enlargement accompanies heart failure. Tissue diagnosis relies on biopsy with apple green staining, while strain imaging shows **apical sparing** and iron overload follows transfusion history in thalassaemia. Sarcoid disease can present with conduction block and responds to steroids, so distinguish restriction from constrictive pericarditis using respiratory signs, septal motion and catheter tracings. Use diuretics cautiously to protect preload and refer selected patients for transplantation.
steps.say: The ventricle stays normal in thickness yet feels rigid, so filling fails while both atria enlarge under pressure. Amyloid disease suggests itself through carpal tunnel symptoms and tongue enlargement, and biopsy confirms the diagnosis with special staining. Strain imaging reveals preserved apical contraction while iron overload follows repeated transfusions. Sarcoidosis declares itself through heart block and usually improves with steroid treatment. Doctors separate restriction from constriction by watching breathing effects and catheter tracings, and they dose diuretics gently to preserve filling.

steps.tx: Myocarditis follows a viral illness with flu-like symptoms, presenting with chest pain, raised troponin and clean coronary arteries. Magnetic resonance imaging supports the diagnosis when oedema meets Lake Louise criteria, while arrhythmia with heart block or ventricular tachycardia signals **electrical instability**. Fulminant cases may need mechanical support as a bridge to recovery, and **endomyocardial biopsy** guides treatment when the course stays unclear. Advise rest from sport for three to six months, recognise Takotsubo ballooning after stress as a mimic that recovers, and follow survivors with echocardiography and rhythm monitoring.
steps.say: Infection injures the heart muscle days after fever settles, and patients report chest discomfort with troponin release although angiography shows open arteries. Resonance imaging detects swelling that matches established diagnostic criteria, while rhythm disturbances warn of electrical fragility. Severe inflammation sometimes demands temporary mechanical support until the ventricle recovers. Doctors advise months away from strenuous sport and keep survivors under regular imaging and rhythm surveillance.
